newsitem.title: USA: Birth control pill doesn't raise breast cancer risk.
newsitem.headline: Birth control pill doesn't raise breast cancer risk.

text.p: Women who take the pill for contraception do not increase their long-term risk of breast cancer, according to a study released on Tuesday.

Scientists found that women showed no increase in breast cancer 10 or more years after they stopped taking the pill, regardless of a family's history of breast cancer, ethnicity, age or country of origin.

"This study answers the major outstanding question we had about the pill -- does it have any persistent effect on breast cancer long after women stop taking it?" Dr. Valerie Beral, chief of the Cancer Epidemiology Unit at Oxford University in Britain, said in a statement.

Beral, who led the effort to combine 54 studies on 150,000 women from 25 countries, said the results were true regardless of how long the women took the pill and what type of pill they used, but researchers observed a very small increase in breast cancer among current and recent oral contraceptive users.

U.S. birth control expert Dr. Carolyn Westhoff told a news conference a possible explanation for this was that doctors who prescribed the pill were more likely to ask for mammograms, which detect breast tumours. She noted that cancer was a disease that developed over many years and that if the pill caused cancer it would not be seen immediately.

"This study had thousands of women in each of the different sub-groups one might have questions about and none of those particular types of women or patterns of use were associated with any risk," said Westhoff, director for family planning at Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Centre in New York.

She wrote an editorial in the journal Contraception on the study, a rare collaboration by more than 200 scientists. Some of the analyses had appeared in The Lancet medical journal. It was funded by the Imperial Cancer Research Fund in Britain.
